name: Double eyelid surgery (Asian blepharoplasty)

lead: Double eyelid surgery forms a crease in the upper eyelid for people whose lids lack one. The payoff is a defined lid line and eyes that look larger and more open.

It is among the most popular cosmetic procedures in many East Asian countries, particularly South Korea, with operations typically lasting 30 to 60 minutes. The literature is large but mostly surgical case series, including patient-reported outcome studies such as a FACE-Q validation of 200 cases.

paras: Surgeons use incisional approaches, which fix the skin to deeper lid structures through a cut, and suture approaches that use buried stitches. It is often combined with epicanthoplasty. Stitches are typically removed after 5 to 7 days, and the crease settles as swelling goes down.
The literature describes static or overly depressed folds, multiple folds, asymmetry and failed folds that need revision, plus suture-related problems with buried-suture methods.

angle.text: Double eyelid surgery forms an upper-lid crease, giving more lid definition and a larger, more open-looking eye. The result is visible after healing. It is among the most commonly performed cosmetic procedures in East Asia, studied mostly in surgical case series.

lead: Double eyelid surgery, also called Asian or East Asian blepharoplasty, supratarsal fold creation or double eyelidplasty, is an operation that forms a crease in an upper eyelid that naturally lacks one. The crease lets the lid fold back as the eye opens, which proponents say makes the eyes look larger, more open and more expressive.[1][2] Surgical authors describe the Asian upper lid as often lacking a superior palpebral fold, with abundant fat, pretarsal skin laxity and a medial epicanthal fold.[2]

Wikipedia reports that the share of East Asian women who naturally have an upper-lid crease varies by study, from about 41 percent of Koreans to 70-83 percent of Chinese and Japanese, so the operation gives a single-lidded person a feature that many of their peers already have.[1] It is described as among the most commonly performed aesthetic procedures in Taiwan, South Korea and other parts of East Asia, and it is also performed in northeast Indian states such as Assam.[1][3]

Methods fall into incisional techniques, in which the surgeon opens the lid and fixes the crease to deeper structures, and non-incisional (buried suture) techniques. Epicanthoplasty, which modifies the inner-corner fold, is often added.[1][4][5] The published literature consists mostly of surgical technique reports and case series, along with patient-reported outcome work such as FACE-Q and a few small randomised studies.[6][7][8]

paras: Authors describe the characteristic features of the Asian upper eyelid as lack of a superior palpebral fold, abundant fat, pretarsal skin laxity and a medial epicanthal fold, and report that many Asians regard double eyelids as attractive.[2] A review describes the anatomy of the Asian upper eyelid, patient assessment, an external incisional technique and pitfalls.[9]

Wikipedia distinguishes double eyelid surgery in younger patients, aimed at creating a fold, from blepharoplasty in older patients, which can also remove surplus skin; a 2022 review likewise notes that in younger patients the goal often centres on creating the supratarsal fold while in older patients surgeons also assess dermatochalasis, ptosis and brow ptosis.[3][10] A review of cultural and aesthetic issues discusses how surgeons define an Asian aesthetic ideal and handle the question of preserving ethnic identity.[11]

The anatomical difference from Western upper-lid surgery is that in many Asian patients the crease position must be fixed with sutures to the levator aponeurosis or septoaponeurotic junction, whereas in Western patients removing redundant skin is often enough to produce a crease.[1]

Wikipedia credits Kotaro Mikamo with first performing the operation in Japan in 1896, in the period after the Meiji Restoration.[1] Interpretations differ: one view sometimes held in the West is that the surgery aimed to westernise Japanese eyes, whereas Mikamo recorded that most Japanese women (82-83 percent in his account) already had double eyelids and described the single lid as monotonous and expressionless, suggesting a motivation rooted in existing Japanese aesthetics.[1]

The word blepharoplasty itself dates to 1818, per Wikipedia.[3] Later decades produced the techniques described in the modern literature, including orbicularis-to-levator fixation,[12] corrective strategies after failed revisions (2004),[13] and the 2013 septoaponeurosis junctional thickening method.[14]

Wikipedia describes two main families. The non-incisional (suture ligation) approach places sutures through the lid at the upper tarsal margin so that subdermal tissue adheres to the levator aponeurosis. It is quicker, with faster recovery and fewer complications, but tends to give a static crease that may soften over time, and buried sutures can irritate the cornea.[1] A review of non-incisional methods says the authors prefer a full-thickness single continuous suture with 7-0 nylon and that careful patient selection reduces loss of the crease.[15]

The incisional method makes a lid incision, removes some skin, fat or muscle as needed, and builds the crease through deeper fixation. Wikipedia says it gives a more dynamic and permanent crease and can address excess skin and fat, but takes longer to recover from and carries a risk of lagophthalmos if too much tissue is removed.[1] Variants include orbicularis oculi to levator aponeurosis fixation,[12] and a septoaponeurosis junctional thickening technique reported in 680 patients and designed to give a dynamic fold rather than a static overdepressed one.[14]

Epicanthoplasty is often added when the inner-corner fold interferes with the result; Y-V advancement, lazy S-curve and comparative techniques have been described.[2][4][5] Practitioners include plastic surgeons, facial plastic surgeons, otolaryngologists, oral and maxillofacial surgeons and oculoplastic ophthalmologists.[1]

For men, a 2024 review addresses Asian male blepharoplasty and rhinoplasty, emphasising distinct anatomical and aesthetic considerations for male patients.[16] In aging lids, infrabrow excision may add functional and aesthetic benefit when lateral brow ptosis and hooding are present.[10] Subbrow blepharoplasty has been combined with double eyelid surgery in a registered study of Asian women.[17]

Wikipedia states the procedure carries some risk of complications but is generally safe in expert hands.[1] Reported problems in the literature include static folds,[14] multiple upper-lid folds requiring correction,[18] lagophthalmos from over-resection,[1] suture-related corneal irritation with buried-suture methods,[1] and failed or lost creases requiring corrective revision.[13][19]

A retrospective study validated FACE-Q appearance satisfaction scales for minor-incision double-eyelid blepharoplasty in 200 young Asian patients, providing a patient-reported way to track how people feel about the result.[6]

Wikipedia reports that many foreigners travel to South Korea for the procedure, with cost estimates of roughly US$2,000 to $4,000 depending on technique and surgeon.[3] A letter in Aesthetic Plastic Surgery titled 'Double-Eyelid Surgery: a Neglected Mirror Perspective' shows the practice is also debated in the surgical literature.[20] In forum discussions, double eyelid surgery is cited as an example of cosmetic surgery being popular in Japan and Korea.[21]

Human evidence is dominated by surgical case series and technique reports.[2][4][13][18][14] A FACE-Q validation study covered 200 patients.[6] Randomised studies have also been published: a 2026 randomised trial of 90 patients with single eyelids tested double-eyelid blepharoplasty combined with levator palpebrae superioris release against conventional open surgery as a way to correct habitual eyebrow and forehead elevation when opening the eyes,[7] and a 2025 randomised study of 60 people compared a modified Park double eyelid technique plus a flying-tail incision for upper-lid skin laxity with a control group.[8] A registered, unrandomised study (NCT04001660, 30 participants) examined subbrow blepharoplasty combined with double eyelid surgery in Asian women.[17] Large head-to-head comparisons of the main techniques have not been published.

timeline.event: Kotaro Mikamo performs the first double eyelid operation in Japan.[1]
Strategies for corrective surgery after failed Asian blepharoplasty published.[13]
Septoaponeurosis junctional thickening technique reported in 680 patients.[14]
FACE-Q scales validated for double-eyelid blepharoplasty in young Asians.[6]
Review on Asian male blepharoplasty and rhinoplasty published.[16]
